Case Report
Paraneoplastic sti ﬀ person syndrome with small cell carcinoma of the
bladder and anti-Ri antibodies
Asier de Albóniga-Chindurza a,⁎
, Elena Riva b, Adolfo Jiménez-Huete b, Francesc Graus c,
Oriol Franch b
a Hospital Ramón y Cajal, Department of Neurology, Colmenar Viejo Road, km 9100, CP 28034, Madrid, Spain
b Hospital Ruber Internacional, Department of Neurology, La Masó Street, 38, CP 28034, Madrid, Spain
c Hospital Clínic de Barcelona, Department of Neurology, Villarroel Street, 170, CP 08036, Barcelona, Spain
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Neuroimmunology
Paraneoplastic
Stiﬀ person
ABSTRACT
The sti ﬀ person syndrome is a rare neurological disorder, di ﬃcult to diagnose and to treat. Paraneoplastic
patients usually present amphiphysin antibodies but the association with anti-Ri antibodies is less known. We
present a case report of paraneoplastic SPS, small cell carcinoma of the bladder and anti-Ri antibodies.
1. Introduction
Stiﬀ person syndrome (SPS) is a neurological disorder characterized
by hypertonia and rigidity of the extremities and the trunk that leads to
a restricted range of motion, slow voluntary movements, muscle hy-
pertrophy and acquisition of abnormal postures such as lumbar hy-
perlordosis. Patients also develop painful muscle spasms that may be
triggered by emotional upset, startle (tactile, auditory and visual sti-
muli) or by sudden movements generated by muscle contractions of
adjacent muscles. Electromyography (EMG) shows a continuous motor-
unit activity, despite attempted relaxation. SPS has an estimated pre-
valence of 1–2 cases per million, and it is more frequent in women, with
a mean age of onset of 45 years old. Although the pathogenesis is not
well identi ﬁed, it is considered autoimmune based on the presence of
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies. Anti-GAD would cause
an imbalance between the catecholaminergic excitatory and GAD in-
hibitory pathways, that control the activity of spinal cord motoneurons
[1]. Small cell carcinoma of the bladder (SCCB) is a very uncommon
neuroendocrine tumor, with a poor prognosis even when it is surgically
resectable. In contrast to small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), it has a low
incidence of paraneoplastic disorders.
2. Case report
A 46-year-old man presented with progressive gait disorder, sec-
ondary to sti ﬀness with pain and spontaneous muscular spasms in his
lower limbs. The pain subsided but the stiﬀ ness progressively worsened.
Symptoms increased in open spaces and in nervous situations. He was
startled excessively when he heard some unexpected noise. On neuro-
logical examination, he had proximal stiﬀ ness in both legs, with im-
possibility of mobilization due to rigidity which caused that he was
completely unable to walk. Myotatic re ﬂexes were exalted, and he had
bilateral ﬂexor plantar responses. He was being followed up by
Oncology for a SCCB, stage IV (T3b, N2, M0), diagnosed 15 months
earlier, and treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (methotrexate,
vinblastine, doxorubicin and cisplatine) and surgery. He had been in
remission until that moment. At the onset of the neurological symp-
toms, lymph node relapse was detected by PET/CT. EMG of lower limbs
showed a continuous motor activity pattern ( Fig. 1 ). Anti-neuronal
antibodies were obtained in serum and cerebrospinal ﬂuid, resulting

anti-Ri positive, anti-GAD, anti-GlyR and antiamphiphysin negative.
Spine and brain MRI with and without contrast were both unremark-
able. Because of tumor relapse, second line of chemotherapy (cisplatin
and etoposide) and local radiotherapy were started until full remission
was achieved. Along he was receiving antineoplastic therapy and
treatment with muscle relaxants (combining diazepam 5 –25 mg, and
baclofen 10– 30 mg, depending on the clinical evolution), he was also
improving ambulation and decreasing stiﬀ ness until disappearance. He
was diagnosed of paraneoplastic SPS, with SCCB and anti-Ri antibodies.
Two years later, the neurological symptoms reappeared rapidly. Several
weeks later, a local and lymph node relapse was detected, with ex-
tensive invasion of the urinary tract and secondary obstructive acute

renal failure. He also presented massive deep vein thrombosis. He was
treated with hemodialysis and heparin, but the patient died due to
successive complications.
3. Discussion
Paraneoplastic SPS variants represent less than 10% of all patients
with SPS. Amphiphysin antibodies are the most common ﬁnding in
these cases [ 1]. Anti-Ri antibodies, also called ANNA-2, are antibodies
directed against intracellular antigens, classically associated with on-
cological pathology. Screening by indirect immuno ﬂuorescence tech-
nique, and subsequent con ﬁrmation by immunoblotting are necessary
for its detection. The presence of anti-Ri antibodies in SPS has been
documented in very few cases. Only one without brainstem involve-
ment [2]. Anti-Ri antibodies determination has been described in other
clinical settings, mainly associated with SCLC and breast cancer, and
presenting with opsoclonus, cerebellar and brainstem manifestations.
We have only found two cases in association with bladder cancer, none
of them SPS [ 3,4]. This antibody may not have a direct etiopathogenic
role, but it could rather represent an immunologic epiphenomenon in
response to speci ﬁc antigens exposed by the tumor. However, experi-
mental data in mice show reactivity of these antibodies against an an-
tigen expressed in the brainstem and the ventral medulla [ 5]. At pre-
sent, the current evidence is limited and mainly based on relatively
small retrospective studies with a wide range of clinical characteristics,
and di ﬀerent treatment protocols. Early antitumoral therapy should be
the ﬁrst step in the management of paraneoplastic syndromes due to
antibodies against intracellular antigens. Corticosteroids could be sec-
ondary options. GABA agonists such as diazepam (type-A receptors)
and oral baclofen (type-B receptors) alone or combined are usually
eﬀective for symptomatic relief.
4. Conclusion
We present a paraneoplastic SPS with neuroendocrine SCCB and
anti-Ri antibodies, with documented neurological response to cancer
treatment and muscle relaxants. In our knowledge, SPS has not been
described in bladder cancer to date.
